figures.caption: Table 3: Efficiency and Performance Trade-off on Internal Benchmark. This table compares the wall-clock time and resulting performance. In terms of total computational cost, the Judge baseline consumes approximately 269 GPU Hours (64 GPUs× 4.2h) for training. In contrast, even when including the selection overhead (16 GPUs × 4.4h ≈ 70 GPU Hours), the Top-50% OST pipeline consumes only 224 GPU Hours in total (70 + 154). This achieves a 17% reduction in total compute resources (and a 43% reduction in the expensive training phase) while boosting accuracy by 1.8 points. (†OST or LLM-as-a-Judge selection is a one-time cost).

(a) Under Protocol B (Fixed Compute), the Best-20% subset achieves the highest Average Score (+5.6%), significantly outperforming both the LLM-as-a-Judge baseline and the uncurated Full-SFT setting. This validates the Less is More hypothesis, where prioritizing data density yields superior convergence over mere data quantity. (b) The fine-grained breakdown reveals that while Full-SFT struggles with complex reasoning (e.g., Higher Ed), the OST-selected subsets effectively unlock these capabilities, achieving substantial gains over the Base model.

Figure 1: Overview of the One-Step-Train (OST) Pipeline. The process reformulates selection into three efficient phases: (1) Proxy Scoring: A lightweight proxy model estimates the marginal utility (Δ𝑖 ) of each sample by measuring validation loss reduction after a simulated single gradient update. (2) Ranking & Selection: Samples are ordered by their update utility, filtering a high-value top-𝑝% subset. (3) Target Training: The large target model is fine-tuned exclusively on this subset, effectively reversing negative transfer.

Table 4: Benchmarking Data Selection Strategies. Comparative results on Qwen3-VL series. The table highlights the trade-offs between different selection methods. While the heuristic scoring baseline (DEITA [22] Top-20%) performs competitively and oftenmatches the LLM-as-a-Judge approach, bothmethods fall short on complex logic tasks compared to optimization-grounded methods. Specifically, they struggle with deep reasoning logic (LogicVista), sometimes degrading performance compared to Base. In contrast, OST (Best-20%) consistently improves complex reasoning capabilities (WeMath, LogicVista) and provides the highest average gain across all model scales, effectively countering the negative transfer observed in Full SFT.

Right: The Autocorrelation Function (ACF) indicates no significant dependency between consecutive samples, validating the independent nature of the proxy scoring.

Figure 2: Sanity checks on 10-class MNIST (55K examples) using a linear regression model. (a) IF vs. LOO: Comparison between Influence Function (IF) scores and exact Leave-One-Out (LOO) loss changes for the top-200 influential examples. The strong linear alignment validates IF as a reliable proxy for LOO in this convex setting. (b)–(c) Ranking Agreement: Alignment between our One-Step-Train utility and IF. To establish a rigorous evaluation chain, we first validate IF as a computationally tractable proxy for the prohibitively expensive exact LOO in (a), and subsequently utilize IF as the ground truth to benchmark our OST method. The observed overlap for top-𝑝% and bottom-𝑝% subsets significantly exceeds the random baseline (dashed line). Note that as the selected subset size reaches the total dataset volume (55,000), any two ranking methods will naturally select the entire pool, causing the overlap to predictably converge to 100%.
